meta.rendering_note: All math is KaTeX in \( ... \) spans; \( n \), \( Z \), \( r_n \), \( E_n \) and \( R \) always appear as single KaTeX spans; no raw Unicode math symbols appear anywhere. Orbital energies \( E_n \) are always negative, while radii, speeds, wavelengths and ionization energies are always non-negative. Every numeric answer terminates cleanly or is a clean order-of-magnitude value.

topics.name: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of the Atom
topics.summary: In the Geiger–Marsden experiment, alpha particles (charge \( +2e \)) were fired at a very thin gold foil. The overwhelming majority passed straight through with little or no deflection, so an atom is mostly empty space. Only a tiny fraction were scattered through large angles, and an even smaller fraction bounced almost straight back. Rutherford concluded that all the positive charge and nearly all the mass sit in a tiny, dense nucleus, about \( 10^{4} \) to \( 10^{5} \) times smaller than the atom, disproving Thomson's plum-pudding model. The aim of an incoming particle is described by its impact parameter \( b \): smaller \( b \) means a larger scattering angle, and \( b=0 \) (head-on) sends the particle back through \( 180^\circ \). In a head-on collision the alpha particle stops at the distance of closest approach \( r_0 \), where all its kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy; \( r_0 \) gives an upper limit on the nuclear size. Rutherford's model, however, was classically unstable: an orbiting electron should radiate and spiral into the nucleus.
key_formulas: Smaller \( b \) gives larger scattering angle; \( b=0 \) gives \( 180^\circ \)
topics.worked_example: A 7.9 MeV alpha particle hits a gold nucleus (\( Z=79 \)) head-on. With \( \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9} \) N·m\( ^{2} \)/C\( ^{2} \) and \( e=1.6\times10^{-19} \) C: \( r_0=\dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times2\times79\times1.6\times10^{-19}}{7.9\times10^{6}}=2.88\times10^{-14} \) m.
common_mistakes: Claiming most alpha particles are strongly deflected — most pass straight through
Reading the result as support for uniformly spread charge (plum-pudding)
Dropping the factor of \( 2 \) in \( r_0 \) (the alpha particle's charge is \( 2e \))
Confusing the closest-approach distance \( r_0 \) with the impact parameter \( b \), or thinking larger \( b \) means larger deflection

topics.name: Bohr's Postulates and the Bohr Model: Radius, Velocity, and Energy of Orbits
topics.summary: Bohr kept Rutherford's nucleus but added three postulates. First, the electron moves only in certain stationary orbits in which it does not radiate. Second, in these orbits its angular momentum is quantized: \( mv_nr_n=\dfrac{nh}{2\pi} \). Third, light is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between orbits, with \( h\nu=E_i-E_f \). For a hydrogen-like (single-electron) ion of atomic number \( Z \), these give \( r_n=0.529\dfrac{n^2}{Z} \) Å, \( v_n=2.18\times10^{6}\dfrac{Z}{n} \) m/s and \( E_n=-\dfrac{13.6Z^2}{n^2} \) eV. The three quantities scale differently: radius grows with \( n^2 \) and shrinks with \( Z \); speed falls with \( n \) (the electron is slower in higher orbits) and rises with \( Z \); energy becomes less negative as \( n \) grows and more negative as \( Z \) grows. In any orbit, kinetic energy is \( -E_n \) and potential energy is \( 2E_n \). The model applies only to H, He\( ^{+} \), Li\( ^{2+} \) and similar one-electron systems.
common_mistakes: Thinking the electron speeds up in higher orbits — \( v_n\propto\dfrac{1}{n} \)
Writing \( r_n\propto\dfrac{Z}{n^2} \) or forgetting to divide by \( Z \)
Using \( Z \) instead of \( Z^2 \) in \( E_n \)
Dropping the negative sign of \( E_n \)

topics.name: Energy Levels, Excitation, Ionization, and Atomic Transitions
topics.summary: Each allowed orbit has a fixed energy \( E_n \), all negative because the electron is bound; \( E_n=0 \) corresponds to a free electron at rest (\( n=\infty \)). For hydrogen the levels are \( -13.6 \), \( -3.4 \), about \( -1.51 \), \( -0.85 \) eV and so on, crowding together just below zero. Excitation moves the electron to a higher level and needs exactly the energy difference, for example 10.2 eV from \( n=1 \) to \( n=2 \). A photon is absorbed only if its energy matches such a difference exactly. Ionization energy is the positive energy needed to take the electron from a given level to \( n=\infty \): 13.6 eV from hydrogen's ground state, \( 13.6Z^2 \) eV for a hydrogen-like ion. If a photon has more than the ionization energy, the extra appears as kinetic energy of the freed electron. When excited atoms fall back, each downward jump emits a photon of energy \( E_i-E_f \); from level \( n \) up to \( \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} \) different lines are possible.
key_formulas: Ionization energy from level \( n \) \( =0-E_n=\dfrac{13.6Z^2}{n^2} \) eV
Number of lines from level \( n \): \( \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} \)
topics.worked_example: Li\( ^{2+} \) (\( Z=3 \)): \( E_1=-122.4 \) eV and \( E_2=-30.6 \) eV. The 2 to 1 photon carries \( 91.8 \) eV, and ionizing from \( n=2 \) needs \( 30.6 \) eV.
common_mistakes: Reporting ionization energy as negative
Using \( |E_n| \) of the upper level as the excitation energy instead of the difference
Assuming a photon can be partly absorbed when its energy matches no level gap
Forgetting the \( Z^2 \) factor for He\( ^{+} \) and Li\( ^{2+} \)

topics.name: Hydrogen Spectral Series: Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, and Pfund
topics.summary: When hydrogen's electron falls from a higher level \( n_2 \) to a lower level \( n_1 \), the emitted line obeys the Rydberg formula \( \dfrac{1}{\lambda}=RZ^2\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2}-\dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right) \), with \( R=1.097\times10^{7} \) m\( ^{-1} \) and \( n_2>n_1 \). Lines are grouped into series by their final level: Lyman (\( n_1=1 \), ultraviolet), Balmer (\( n_1=2 \), the only series with visible lines, partly extending into the near ultraviolet), Paschen (\( n_1=3 \)), Brackett (\( n_1=4 \)) and Pfund (\( n_1=5 \)), the last three entirely infrared. Within a series, the longest wavelength comes from the smallest jump, \( n_1+1 \) to \( n_1 \), and the shortest wavelength, the series limit, comes from \( n_2\to\infty \). Lines crowd together towards the limit. The photon energy at a series limit equals the ionization energy from that series' final level; for example, \( hcR=13.6 \) eV. For hydrogen-like ions the whole pattern is scaled by \( Z^2 \).
topics.worked_example: Balmer \( H_\alpha \) (3 to 2): \( \dfrac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{9}\right)=\dfrac{5R}{36} \), so \( \lambda=\dfrac{36}{5R} \). Balmer limit: \( \dfrac{1}{\lambda}=\dfrac{R}{4} \), which is \( 2.75\times10^{6} \) m\( ^{-1} \) for \( R=1.1\times10^{7} \) m\( ^{-1} \).
common_mistakes: Swapping \( n_1 \) and \( n_2 \), which gives a negative wavenumber
Naming a series by its starting level instead of its final level
Crediting a series other than Balmer with visible lines
Computing the series limit from \( n_1+1 \) to \( n_1 \) (that is the longest wavelength) instead of \( n_2\to\infty \)

topics.name: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Quantization Condition, and Limitations of the Bohr Model
topics.summary: de Broglie explained Bohr's quantization rule by treating the electron as a wave with \( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv} \). For the wave to survive going round an orbit, it must join smoothly with itself as a standing wave, so the circumference must hold exactly a whole number of wavelengths: \( 2\pi r_n=n\lambda \). Substituting \( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv_n} \) gives \( mv_nr_n=\dfrac{nh}{2\pi} \), exactly Bohr's postulate. The number of wavelengths in orbit \( n \) is \( n \) itself, and in hydrogen \( \lambda\propto n \), since the electron slows in higher orbits. Despite its successes, Bohr's model has clear limitations. It works only for single-electron (hydrogen-like) systems and fails for multi-electron atoms because it cannot include electron-electron repulsion. It does not explain the relative intensities of spectral lines or their fine structure. And its sharply defined orbits, with precise position and momentum at every instant, contradict Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, so later quantum mechanics replaced them.
topics.worked_example: Hydrogen \( n=2 \): \( r_2=2.116 \) Å, so \( \lambda=\dfrac{2\pi\times2.116}{2}=2.116\pi \) Å, and exactly 2 wavelengths fit around the orbit.
common_mistakes: Allowing a half-integer number of wavelengths, or an inequality, instead of an exact whole-number fit
Using \( \pi r_n \) instead of the full circumference \( 2\pi r_n \)
Claiming Bohr's model works for multi-electron atoms such as neutral He
Believing Bohr's model needed no correction from later quantum mechanics

questions.topic: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of the Atom
questions.question: In the Geiger–Marsden experiment, alpha particles are fired at a thin gold foil. What happens to the overwhelming majority of them?
options: They pass straight through with little or no deflection
They are deflected through large angles
They bounce almost straight back towards the source
They are absorbed and stopped inside the foil
questions.explanation:
Almost all alpha particles go through the foil essentially undeflected.

This means most of the volume of an atom is empty space, with nothing massive enough in the way to push the alpha particle aside.

Only a very small fraction are scattered through large angles, and an even smaller fraction bounce back.
questions.hint: Think about what the result tells you about how much of the atom is empty.
distractor_logic: Large-angle scattering happens to only a tiny fraction; claiming it for most particles is the central misreading of the experiment
Back-scattering is the rarest outcome of all, not the typical one
Gold foil thin enough for the experiment lets alpha particles pass; absorption was not what was observed

questions.topic: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of the Atom
questions.question: A very small fraction of alpha particles were found to bounce almost straight back from the gold foil. What did Rutherford conclude from this?
options: Positive charge is spread uniformly throughout the atom
The atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus
The electrons are packed together at the centre of the atom
The atom is mostly filled with solid matter
questions.explanation:
To turn a fast, heavy alpha particle around, it must meet a very strong repulsive force.

That is only possible if the atom's positive charge and almost all its mass are concentrated in a very small region — the nucleus.

A uniformly spread charge (Thomson's plum-pudding model) could never produce such a strong force.
questions.hint: What kind of charge distribution could reverse a heavy, fast, positively charged particle?
distractor_logic: This is the plum-pudding picture, which the experiment disproved because a spread-out charge cannot reverse an alpha particle
Electrons are far too light to turn back an alpha particle, and they are not at the centre
Most alpha particles pass straight through, so the atom is mostly empty, not solid

questions.topic: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of the Atom
questions.question: In Rutherford's experiment, roughly what fraction of alpha particles were scattered by more than \( 90^\circ \)?
questions.explanation:
Only about 1 alpha particle in 8000 was deflected by more than \( 90^\circ \).

This rarity shows that the nucleus occupies only a tiny part of the atom, so a close encounter with it is very unlikely.

But the fact that it happens at all shows the nucleus exists.
questions.hint: Large-angle scattering is real but extremely rare.
distractor_logic: Half would mean the nucleus fills much of the atom, which contradicts the mostly-undeflected result
1 in 10 is far too common for scattering off a tiny nucleus
Some particles were indeed scattered back; that observation is the whole basis of the nuclear model

questions.topic: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of the Atom
questions.question: An atom has a size of order \( 10^{-10} \) m, while Rutherford's experiment showed the nucleus is of order \( 10^{-15} \) m to \( 10^{-14} \) m. Roughly how many times smaller is the nucleus than the atom?
questions.explanation:
Divide the atom's size by the nucleus's size: \( \dfrac{10^{-10}}{10^{-14}}=10^{4} \) and \( \dfrac{10^{-10}}{10^{-15}}=10^{5} \).

So the nucleus is roughly \( 10^{4} \) to \( 10^{5} \) times smaller than the atom — which is why most of the atom is empty space.
questions.hint: Subtract the powers of ten.
distractor_logic: A factor of 10 would make the nucleus a large part of the atom, and many more particles would be deflected
If the nucleus were atom-sized, nearly every alpha particle would be scattered
This adds the exponents instead of subtracting them

questions.topic: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of the Atom
questions.question: For a head-on collision (impact parameter \( b=0 \)), which expression gives the distance of closest approach \( r_0 \) of an alpha particle with kinetic energy \( KE \) to a nucleus of atomic number \( Z \)?
questions.explanation:
At closest approach the alpha particle momentarily stops, so all its kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy.

The alpha particle carries charge \( 2e \) and the nucleus \( Ze \), so \( KE=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{(2e)(Ze)}{r_0} \).

Rearranging gives \( r_0=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{2Ze^2}{KE} \).
questions.hint: Set kinetic energy equal to the Coulomb potential energy between charges \( 2e \) and \( Ze \).
distractor_logic: Drops the factor of 2 — the alpha particle's charge is \( 2e \), not \( e \)
Squares the kinetic energy; energy balance is linear in \( KE \)
Puts \( KE \) in the numerator, which would make faster particles stop farther away — the opposite of reality

questions.topic: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of the Atom
questions.question: Why was a very thin gold foil used in the alpha-scattering experiment?
options: Because gold is radioactive and adds its own alpha particles
So that each alpha particle is scattered at most once, making the results easy to interpret
So that the foil absorbs all the slow alpha particles
Because a thick foil would be completely transparent to alpha particles
questions.explanation:
In a thin foil, an alpha particle usually meets at most one nucleus closely.

A single scattering event can be analysed cleanly with Coulomb's law, so the observed angles directly reveal the nucleus.

Gold can be beaten into extremely thin sheets, which is why it was chosen.
questions.hint: Think about how many nuclei a particle might meet in a thick versus a thin foil.
distractor_logic: Gold is not radioactive; the alpha particles came from a separate radioactive source
The foil's purpose was scattering, not filtering out slow particles
A thicker foil stops or multiply-scatters more particles; it is not more transparent

questions.topic: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of the Atom
questions.question: In alpha-particle scattering, what is the impact parameter \( b \)?
options: The smallest distance the alpha particle reaches from the nucleus during its motion
The radius of the gold nucleus
The perpendicular distance of the alpha particle's initial velocity line from the centre of the nucleus
The distance the alpha particle travels inside the foil
questions.explanation:
The impact parameter \( b \) is measured before the interaction: it is how far the particle's original straight-line path would miss the nucleus's centre.

It is different from the distance of closest approach \( r_0 \), which is reached during the motion.

Only for a head-on collision is \( b=0 \).
questions.hint: It describes the aim of the particle, not where it ends up.
distractor_logic: This is the distance of closest approach; confusing it with \( b \) is a classic trap
The nuclear radius is a property of the target, not of the particle's aim
The path length in the foil has nothing to do with how the particle is aimed at one nucleus

questions.topic: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of the Atom
questions.question: What is the charge of the alpha particle used in Rutherford's experiment?
questions.explanation:
An alpha particle is a helium nucleus: 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

Its charge is therefore \( +2e \).

This is where the factor of \( 2 \) in \( r_0=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{2Ze^2}{KE} \) comes from.
questions.hint: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus.
distractor_logic: That is the charge of a proton, which has only one proton
An alpha particle is positively charged; that is why the positive nucleus repels it
A neutral particle would not be repelled by the nucleus at all

questions.topic: Bohr's Postulates and the Bohr Model: Radius, Velocity, and Energy of Orbits
questions.question: Which statement is Bohr's quantization condition for the angular momentum of an electron in orbit \( n \)?
questions.explanation:
Bohr postulated that the electron can only occupy orbits in which its angular momentum is a whole-number multiple of \( \dfrac{h}{2\pi} \).

So \( mv_nr_n=\dfrac{nh}{2\pi} \), with \( n=1,2,3,\ldots \)
questions.hint: Angular momentum comes in whole-number multiples of \( \dfrac{h}{2\pi} \).
distractor_logic: Puts \( n \) in the denominator, so angular momentum would shrink in higher orbits
Omits the \( 2\pi \); the quantum unit is \( \dfrac{h}{2\pi} \), not \( h \)
Uses \( 4\pi \) instead of \( 2\pi \), halving the quantum unit

questions.topic: Bohr's Postulates and the Bohr Model: Radius, Velocity, and Energy of Orbits
questions.question: For a hydrogen-like ion, how does the orbit radius \( r_n \) depend on \( n \) and \( Z \)?
questions.explanation:
Bohr's model gives \( r_n=0.529\dfrac{n^2}{Z} \) Å.

Radius grows as \( n^2 \) — higher orbits are much bigger.

Radius shrinks with \( Z \) — a more highly charged nucleus pulls the electron closer.
questions.hint: Higher orbits are larger; a stronger nucleus pulls the electron in.
distractor_logic: Reverses both dependencies, so higher orbits would be smaller
Uses \( n \) instead of \( n^2 \), underestimating how fast orbits grow
Makes radius grow with \( Z \), but a larger nuclear charge pulls the electron closer

questions.topic: Bohr's Postulates and the Bohr Model: Radius, Velocity, and Energy of Orbits
questions.question: As \( n \) increases in the hydrogen atom, what happens to the electron's orbital speed?
options: It stays the same in every orbit
questions.explanation:
Bohr's model gives \( v_n\propto\dfrac{Z}{n} \).

So the electron moves slower in higher orbits, even though those orbits have higher (less negative) energy.

In the ground state of hydrogen the speed is about \( 2.18\times10^{6} \) m/s, and in \( n=2 \) it is half of that.
questions.hint: Farther from the nucleus, the attraction is weaker, so less speed is needed.
distractor_logic: The common intuition that higher-energy orbits mean faster motion — the electron actually slows down
Speed does depend on \( n \); only angular momentum steps up in equal units
The \( \dfrac{1}{n^2} \) dependence belongs to energy, not speed

questions.topic: Bohr's Postulates and the Bohr Model: Radius, Velocity, and Energy of Orbits
questions.question: Using \( r_n=0.529\,n^2 \) Å for hydrogen, what is the radius of the \( n=2 \) orbit?
questions.hint: Square \( n \) before multiplying.
distractor_logic: Multiplies by \( n \) instead of \( n^2 \)
Divides by \( n^2 \), as if higher orbits were smaller
Multiplies by \( n^3 \) instead of \( n^2 \)

questions.topic: Bohr's Postulates and the Bohr Model: Radius, Velocity, and Energy of Orbits
questions.question: What is the energy of the electron in the ground state of the hydrogen atom?
questions.explanation:
For hydrogen, \( E_n=-\dfrac{13.6}{n^2} \) eV.

With \( n=1 \), \( E_1=-13.6 \) eV.

The negative sign means the electron is bound to the nucleus.
questions.hint: Put \( n=1 \) into \( E_n=-\dfrac{13.6}{n^2} \) eV and keep the sign.
distractor_logic: Drops the negative sign; a positive orbital energy would mean the electron is not bound
This is \( E_2 \), the first excited state
This is the potential energy in the ground state, not the total energy

questions.topic: Bohr's Postulates and the Bohr Model: Radius, Velocity, and Energy of Orbits
questions.question: Which expression gives the energy \( E_n \) of the electron in orbit \( n \) of a hydrogen-like ion with atomic number \( Z \)?
questions.explanation:
Bohr's energy for a single-electron ion is \( E_n=-\dfrac{13.6Z^2}{n^2} \) eV.

It depends on \( Z^2 \) because both the nuclear charge and the smaller orbit strengthen the binding.

It is negative for every bound state.
questions.hint: Energy depends on the square of the nuclear charge.
distractor_logic: Uses \( Z \) instead of \( Z^2 \)
Inverts the fraction, making higher orbits more tightly bound
Positive sign would mean the electron is unbound

questions.topic: Bohr's Postulates and the Bohr Model: Radius, Velocity, and Energy of Orbits
questions.question: According to Bohr's postulates, an electron moving in one of the allowed (stationary) orbits
options: radiates energy continuously and slowly spirals inwards
radiates only when its speed is greatest
absorbs energy continuously from the nucleus
questions.explanation:
Bohr's first postulate: in a stationary orbit the electron does not radiate, even though it is accelerating.

Radiation is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between orbits.

This postulate is what makes the atom stable.
questions.hint: Stationary orbits are exactly what make the atom stable.
distractor_logic: This is the classical prediction for Rutherford's atom that Bohr rejected
Speed is constant in a circular orbit, and no radiation is emitted in any stationary orbit
The electron's energy stays fixed in a stationary orbit

questions.topic: Bohr's Postulates and the Bohr Model: Radius, Velocity, and Energy of Orbits
questions.question: By Bohr's frequency condition, when an electron jumps from an initial level of energy \( E_i \) to a lower level of energy \( E_f \), the emitted photon has frequency \( \nu \) given by
questions.explanation:
The photon carries away exactly the energy the atom loses.

So \( h\nu=E_i-E_f \), which is positive because \( E_i \) is higher than \( E_f \).
questions.hint: The photon's energy equals the energy difference between levels.
distractor_logic: Adding the two (negative) energies has no physical meaning for the photon
Forgets Planck's constant — energy and frequency are linked by \( h \)
A ratio of energies is dimensionless, not an energy

questions.topic: Energy Levels, Excitation, Ionization, and Atomic Transitions
questions.question: What is the ionization energy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state?
questions.explanation:
Ionization means taking the electron from \( n=1 \) to \( n=\infty \), where \( E_n=0 \).

Energy needed \( =0-(-13.6)=13.6 \) eV.

Ionization energy is always a positive amount of energy that must be supplied.
questions.hint: How much energy lifts the electron from \( -13.6 \) eV up to 0?
distractor_logic: Ionization energy is energy supplied, so it is positive; \( -13.6 \) eV is the ground-state energy itself
This is the energy to reach \( n=2 \), not \( n=\infty \)
This is the ionization energy from \( n=2 \), not from the ground state

questions.topic: Energy Levels, Excitation, Ionization, and Atomic Transitions
questions.question: What is the first excitation energy of hydrogen (from \( n=1 \) to \( n=2 \))?
questions.hint: Subtract the ground-state energy from the \( n=2 \) energy.
distractor_logic: This is just the magnitude of \( E_2 \), not the difference between levels
This is the ionization energy, a jump to \( n=\infty \)
This is the excitation energy to \( n=3 \)

questions.topic: Energy Levels, Excitation, Ionization, and Atomic Transitions
questions.question: What is the energy \( E_n \) of the electron in the \( n=4 \) level of hydrogen?
questions.hint: Divide by \( n^2 \), not \( n \), and keep the minus sign.
distractor_logic: Divides by \( n \) instead of \( n^2 \)
Drops the sign; every bound level has negative energy
Multiplies by \( n^2 \) instead of dividing

questions.topic: Energy Levels, Excitation, Ionization, and Atomic Transitions
questions.question: What is the energy of the electron when it is at \( n=\infty \), i.e. just removed from the atom with no kinetic energy?
questions.explanation:
Using \( E_n=-\dfrac{13.6}{n^2} \) eV, as \( n\to\infty \), \( E_n\to0 \).

Zero energy is the reference for a free electron at rest far from the nucleus.

All bound levels lie below it, so they are negative.
questions.hint: Let \( n \) grow without limit in \( -\dfrac{13.6}{n^2} \).
distractor_logic: This is the ground-state energy, the most tightly bound level, not the free state
A positive value would mean the electron still has kinetic energy after leaving
The energy approaches zero from below; it does not run off to negative infinity

questions.topic: Energy Levels, Excitation, Ionization, and Atomic Transitions
questions.question: Why is the energy of an electron in any Bohr orbit negative?
options: Because the electron is bound to the nucleus, and energy must be supplied to free it
Because the electron's kinetic energy is negative
Because the electron repels the nucleus
Because the electron has negative mass
questions.explanation:
The zero of energy is chosen as a free electron at rest far away.

A bound electron has less energy than that, so its total energy is negative.

The magnitude of this negative energy is the energy needed to free it.
questions.hint: Compare with the energy of a free electron at rest.
distractor_logic: Kinetic energy is never negative; it is the potential energy that is negative
The electron is attracted to the positive nucleus, not repelled
Mass is always positive; the sign comes from binding

questions.topic: Energy Levels, Excitation, Ionization, and Atomic Transitions
questions.question: Hydrogen atoms are excited to the \( n=4 \) level. What is the maximum number of different spectral lines that can be emitted as they return to the ground state?
questions.explanation:
The number of possible lines from level \( n \) is \( \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} \).

For \( n=4 \): \( \dfrac{4\times3}{2}=6 \).

They are 4 to 3, 4 to 2, 4 to 1, 3 to 2, 3 to 1 and 2 to 1.
questions.hint: Count every pair of levels from 1 to 4.
distractor_logic: Counts only the downward steps one level at a time, missing direct jumps
Counts only the number of levels, not the pairs
This is the count for \( n=5 \)

questions.topic: Energy Levels, Excitation, Ionization, and Atomic Transitions
questions.question: An electron in hydrogen moves from \( n=1 \) to \( n=3 \). What does the atom do?
options: It emits a photon of energy \( E_3-E_1 \)
It absorbs energy equal to \( E_3+E_1 \)
It absorbs energy equal to \( E_3-E_1 \)
It neither absorbs nor emits energy
questions.explanation:
Moving to a higher level (less negative energy) needs energy input.

The atom must absorb exactly \( E_3-E_1 \), for example from a photon or a collision.

Emission happens only when the electron drops to a lower level.
questions.hint: Is \( n=3 \) higher or lower in energy than \( n=1 \)?
distractor_logic: Emission happens on a downward jump; this is an upward jump
The energy needed is a difference of levels, not a sum
Any change of level involves exchanging energy

questions.topic: Energy Levels, Excitation, Ionization, and Atomic Transitions
questions.question: What is the ionization energy of the He\( ^{+} \) ion (\( Z=2 \)) in its ground state?
questions.hint: Energy scales as \( Z^2 \).
distractor_logic: Uses \( Z \) instead of \( Z^2 \)
Ignores the nuclear charge and uses hydrogen's value
Ionization energy is supplied energy, so it is positive

questions.topic: Hydrogen Spectral Series: Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, and Pfund
questions.question: All lines of the Lyman series of hydrogen end at which level?
questions.explanation:
A series is named by its final (lower) level \( n_1 \).

Lyman: \( n_1=1 \); Balmer: \( n_1=2 \); Paschen: \( n_1=3 \); Brackett: \( n_1=4 \); Pfund: \( n_1=5 \).
questions.hint: Lyman is the series ending at the lowest possible level.
distractor_logic: This is the Balmer series
This is the Paschen series
This is the Pfund series

questions.topic: Hydrogen Spectral Series: Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, and Pfund
questions.question: Which hydrogen spectral series is the only one with lines in the visible region?
questions.explanation:
Balmer lines (ending at \( n=2 \)) include the red, blue-green and violet lines of hydrogen.

Lyman lies in the ultraviolet; Paschen, Brackett and Pfund lie entirely in the infrared.
questions.hint: It is the series ending at \( n=2 \).
distractor_logic: Lyman lines have large energy gaps and lie in the ultraviolet
Paschen lines lie entirely in the infrared
Pfund lines have tiny energy gaps and lie far in the infrared

questions.topic: Hydrogen Spectral Series: Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, and Pfund
questions.question: Why does every Lyman line have a greater photon energy than every Balmer line?
options: Lyman lines start from higher levels than Balmer lines
Lyman lines are in the visible and Balmer lines are in the infrared
Even the smallest Lyman gap (10.2 eV) is larger than the largest Balmer gap (3.4 eV)
The Rydberg constant is larger for the Lyman series

questions.explanation:

questions.question: For hydrogen, how does the de Broglie wavelength of the electron in orbit \( n \) depend on \( n \)?
questions.explanation:
\( \lambda=\dfrac{2\pi r_n}{n} \) and \( r_n\propto n^2 \).

So \( \lambda\propto\dfrac{n^2}{n}=n \).

This matches \( \lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv_n} \) with \( v_n\propto\dfrac{1}{n} \): a slower electron has a longer wavelength.
questions.hint: Combine \( r_n\propto n^2 \) with \( \lambda=\dfrac{2\pi r_n}{n} \).
distractor_logic: This is the radius dependence, not the wavelength
This would need the electron to speed up in higher orbits
The wavelength does change, because speed changes

questions.topic: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Quantization Condition, and Limitations of the Bohr Model
questions.question: Why can't Bohr's model predict the energy levels of neutral helium?
options: Helium has two electrons, and the model cannot include the repulsion between electrons
The helium nucleus is too heavy for the model
It can, simply by putting \( Z=2 \) into the hydrogen formula
questions.explanation:
Bohr's model treats one electron attracted by a nucleus.

In neutral helium, each electron is also repelled by the other, and the model has no way to handle this.

So it works for He\( ^{+} \) but not neutral He.
questions.hint: How many electrons does neutral helium have?
distractor_logic: Nuclear mass is not the problem; He\( ^{+} \) works fine
The issue is the extra electron, not a lack of orbits

questions.topic: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Quantization Condition, and Limitations of the Bohr Model
questions.question: Which assumption of Bohr's model conflicts with Heisenberg's uncertainty principle?
options: The energy of the atom is quantized
The electron moves in a sharply defined circular orbit with a definite speed
The photon's energy equals the difference between levels
questions.explanation:
A definite circular path means the electron's position and momentum are both known exactly at each instant.

The uncertainty principle says this is impossible.

Energy quantization and the frequency condition survive in modern quantum mechanics.
questions.hint: Which assumption fixes both position and momentum at once?
distractor_logic: Quantized energy remains true in quantum mechanics
The frequency condition is still correct
The positive nucleus comes from Rutherford's experiment and is correct

questions.topic: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Quantization Condition, and Limitations of the Bohr Model
questions.question: Which statement about Bohr's model is correct?
options: It gives the correct energy levels for neutral lithium
It explains the fine structure of spectral lines
It gives the correct energy levels for Li\( ^{2+} \)
It explains the relative intensities of spectral lines
questions.explanation:
Li\( ^{2+} \) has one electron, so it is a hydrogen-like ion and Bohr's formula \( E_n=-\dfrac{13.6Z^2}{n^2} \) eV with \( Z=3 \) works.

questions.question: An alpha particle with kinetic energy 4.5 MeV approaches a tin nucleus (\( Z=50 \)) head-on. Take \( \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}=9\times10^{9} \) N·m\( ^{2} \)/C\( ^{2} \) and \( e=1.6\times10^{-19} \) C. What is the distance of closest approach?

\( r_0=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{2Ze^2}{KE} \) with \( KE=4.5\times10^{6}e \) J.

\( r_0=\dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times100\times1.6\times10^{-19}}{4.5\times10^{6}} \)

\( r_0=\dfrac{1.44\times10^{-7}}{4.5\times10^{6}}=3.2\times10^{-14} \) m
questions.hint: Cancel one factor of \( e \) against the eV-to-joule conversion.
distractor_logic: Drops the factor of 2 for the alpha particle's charge

questions.topic: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of the Atom
questions.question: A 7.9 MeV alpha particle aimed head-on at a gold nucleus (\( Z=79 \)) turns back at \( 2.88\times10^{-14} \) m from its centre, still repelled only by the Coulomb force. What can be concluded about the radius of the gold nucleus?
options: It must be larger than \( 2.88\times10^{-14} \) m
It must be smaller than about \( 2.88\times10^{-14} \) m
questions.explanation:
The alpha particle turned around under pure Coulomb repulsion without touching the nucleus.

So the nuclear surface lies inside the closest-approach distance.

The closest approach therefore gives an upper limit on the nuclear size.
questions.hint: Did the particle reach the nucleus's surface?
distractor_logic: If the nucleus were larger, the particle would have hit it before turning
Closest approach only bounds the size; it does not measure the surface exactly

questions.topic: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of the Atom
questions.question: A proton and an alpha particle with the same kinetic energy are each fired head-on at the same nucleus. What is the ratio of the proton's distance of closest approach to the alpha particle's?
questions.explanation:
In general, \( KE=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\dfrac{q\,Ze}{r_0} \), so \( r_0\propto q \) at fixed \( KE \) and \( Z \).

The proton has \( q=e \) and the alpha particle \( q=2e \).

Ratio \( =\dfrac{e}{2e}=\dfrac{1}{2} \)
questions.hint: The factor 2 in the alpha formula is the alpha particle's charge.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio — the less-charged proton is repelled less and gets closer
Assumes closest approach does not depend on the projectile's charge
Brings in the mass ratio; at equal kinetic energy, mass does not enter \( r_0 \)

\( KE=15.8 \) MeV
questions.hint: Rearrange the closest-approach formula for \( KE \).

questions.question: Two alpha particles of the same energy are scattered by the same nucleus, one through \( 30^\circ \) and the other through \( 90^\circ \). Which statement is correct?
options: The \( 90^\circ \) particle had the smaller impact parameter, and neither had \( b=0 \)
The \( 30^\circ \) particle had the smaller impact parameter
Both had the same impact parameter, equal to the distance of closest approach

Smaller impact parameter means stronger repulsion and a larger scattering angle, so the \( 90^\circ \) particle had the smaller \( b \).

Only \( b=0 \) gives \( 180^\circ \), so both had nonzero \( b \).

Impact parameter and closest-approach distance are different quantities.

\( b=0 \) gives \( 180^\circ \), not \( 90^\circ \)

questions.topic: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of the Atom
questions.question: If Thomson's plum-pudding model (positive charge spread uniformly through the atom) had been correct, what would Geiger and Marsden have observed?
options: Many alpha particles bouncing straight back
All alpha particles deflected by only small angles, with essentially no large-angle scattering
All alpha particles absorbed by the foil
About half the alpha particles deflected by more than \( 90^\circ \)

A spread-out positive charge exerts only a weak force on a passing alpha particle.

So every particle would be nudged by a tiny angle, with no way to turn one around.

The rare large-angle scattering actually seen ruled this model out.

Energy \( =E_2-E_1=-3.4-(-13.6)=10.2 \) eV

questions.question: Which statement correctly traces how models of the atom developed?
options: Rutherford found the nucleus by scattering; Bohr added quantized orbits for stability; later quantum mechanics replaced sharply defined orbits
Bohr found the nucleus by scattering; Rutherford added quantized orbits
Rutherford's model was already stable, so Bohr only added the Rydberg formula
Bohr's orbits are exactly correct and needed no later changes
questions.explanation:
Alpha scattering revealed the nucleus (Rutherford).

Bohr's quantized, non-radiating orbits made the atom stable and explained hydrogen's lines.

Because definite orbits conflict with the uncertainty principle, quantum mechanics later replaced them.
questions.hint: Each step fixed the previous model's biggest failure.
distractor_logic: Swaps the two scientists' contributions
Rutherford's classical atom was unstable
Bohr's model conflicts with the uncertainty principle and fails for multi-electron atoms

questions.topic: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of the Atom
questions.question: If the nuclear charge \( Z \) is increased, what happens to the closest-approach distance \( r_0 \) of an alpha particle of fixed kinetic energy, and to the Bohr radius \( r_1 \) of a hydrogen-like ion?
questions.explanation:
\( r_0\propto Z \): a more strongly charged nucleus stops the repelled alpha particle farther away.

\( r_n\propto\dfrac{n^2}{Z} \): a more strongly charged nucleus pulls the attracted electron closer.

Repulsion and attraction give opposite trends.
questions.hint: One particle is repelled, the other attracted.
distractor_logic: The attracted electron is pulled closer, not pushed out
The repelled alpha particle is stopped farther away
Reverses both dependencies
